segments: so um thanks everybody for coming, I know it's the last slot before lunch so I I will try not to ramble. uh my name is Dan and I'm one of the, one of the founders at Nova lith, and what we, we basically built a, sorry, we basically spent the last year building a thing called Kestrel. and Kestrel is, you know, it's kind of an AI research assistant for people who trade crypto, like on chain stuff, perps, funding rates, all of that. and I think the the honest origin story is that it was not supposed to be a product at all. it was a internal tool. we had like four analysts at Novalit, um, sorry Novalith, and they were spending I don't know, maybe six hours a day just jumping between dashboards, right? looking at wallet flows, looking at what the big wallets were doing on Solana, and then pasting stuff into a doc. and one of our engineers said why don't we just let an LLM do the pasting, and and that was kind of the whole idea. so that was, uh, a year ago, a bit more than a year ago actually, twenty twenty four I think, late twenty twenty four.

and the first version honestly was terrible. it, it could answer questions about a wallet, but it hallucinated a lot, it would say a wallet bought something that it didn't buy, and nobody trusted it, so no one was using it. like literally no one, I I checked the logs and it was me and one other guy. so we we sat there and thought okay, do we kill this or do we, you know, double down. and what we figured out is that the problem wasn't the model, it was that we were giving it a pile of raw data and just hoping. so we rebuilt the whole data layer. we call it the Smart Money tables, which is a very boring name, but it's basically a set of clean tables where every wallet is labeled, and the label is not something the model guesses, it's something we compute. so the agent can ask a question and it's actually grounded in a table, not in vibes. and that, um, that changed it a lot. I'm not saying it's perfect, it's definitely not perfect, but the trust thing got a lot better.

so fast forward to now, uh, we launched publicly about six months back, and we didn't really expect what happened, we thought maybe a couple thousand people would try it. and instead we're at like two hundred thousand users, which, I mean, I still can't really believe that number. and most of them are not professional traders, I want to be clear about that, it's mostly people who are, kind of, curious, they have a bag of something and they want to understand why it's moving. um and the, the weirdest thing is the retention is good, like thirty percent of people who sign up are still there after, after a month, which for this category is I think pretty unusual. I'm not going to claim we know exactly why. my guess is it's because Castrel, Kestrel, gives you an answer that's, like, short and checkable, and you can click through to the table and see the rows. but I'm not sure if that's the real reason, maybe it's just the timing and the market was, was really loud this year.

okay so let me actually show you something instead of just talking. um can everybody see the screen? it's a little small, I'll zoom. so this is the main view, and on the left you've got, uh, the chat, and on the right there's the the table pane. and the first thing I want to show is, so we have this bot we call Grokbot, well, we spell it G R O K, but I think everyone hears it as Crockbot, which is fine, that's what we say internally now too. and Crockbot is basically the part that reads the, the social side. it watches a bunch of accounts and channels, it pulls out claims, like somebody says this token is about to do something, and then it checks the claim against on chain flows. so if someone says whales are accumulating, it goes and looks, and and it tells you whether that's actually true or not. most of the time, honestly, it's not true. it's like, I don't know, maybe one in five claims has anything behind it. which is kind of depressing but it's also the product, right?

and then the second thing, this is SuperTick, um, and I think this one is my favorite. so SuperTick is a feed, it's a, it's a stream of events that we think matter, and we rank them. so a big wallet moves funds to an exchange, that's an event, funding rate flips negative on a perp, that's an event, and SuperTick gives them a score. and before this, a user would have to set up like ten alerts by hand and then ignore them all. now it's just, you open it and the top of the feed is the thing you should care about. we're not saying it predicts the price, it doesn't, I really don't want anyone to leave here thinking that. it just says this is unusual compared to the last, say, thirty days. and I'd say it's still not as proactive as I want, like it doesn't come and tap you on the shoulder yet, you have to go look. that's, that's on the roadmap, I'll get to that.

so what does the loop look like for a normal person, let me just do it live. I type, why is Solana funding so negative right now, and it's thinking, and, uh, okay it comes back and says funding on the major perps has been negative for about, it says, nine days, and that three x more shorts were opened than the usual average. and below that it shows the table. and this part, I I really care about this, every number in the answer has a little link, so you click and you see the rows. um, it took, what, twelve seconds? so that would have taken one of our analysts like ten minutes before, to pull from three dashboards. it's not always that fast, sometimes it just times out and and we show you a sad little error. that's that's the basic loop. any questions on that before I move on? no? okay.

oh wait, actually someone did ask me earlier, in the hallway, about whether the answers are the same for everybody, like does it personalize. and the answer is not really, not yet. we don't keep a profile of you, we kind of decided early on that we didn't want to, because the moment you personalize you start telling people what they want to hear, and and in this business that's dangerous. for now every answer is based on the same tables, and the only thing that changes is your watchlist. and, um, a related thing, somebody else asked can it place trades. no. it can't. we, we explicitly don't do that, there's no wallet connection, there's no keys, and I think that's a decision we'll keep. we looked at it, we actually prototyped it for like two weeks, and then we decided to kill the trade execution feature, because the failure mode is somebody loses their money and then it's your fault, you know?

so the next thing is for the, the more technical people in the room. we have a thing called Kestral Gym and Jupyter, uh, which is, it's basically a notebook environment, you open it and the agent is sitting next to you, and you can say run a backtest of this idea on the last, I don't know, two years of data. and it writes the code, runs it, and shows you the PnL curve. and the gym part is, so the agent can try a bunch of variations on its own, like change the threshold, change the window, and see which of them survives out of sample. I should be careful, um, because backtests lie, everybody knows that, and and the agent can overfit just like a person can. so we put in a bunch of guards, it has to hold back a chunk of data it never sees, and we show you that number first, not last. I think most of the tools out there kind of bury it, and we thought, no, put it at the top.

and then there's the distribution side, which is kind of boring but it matters. a lot of our users don't want to open an app at all, they want it in the, in the Retreat Channel, I mean the Telegram channel, sorry, my brain does that. so you can add the bot to a group and it posts the SuperTick top five every morning, and people just argue about it in the chat. and we didn't really plan for that, we didn't plan for it at all, it was a user who hacked it together with a webhook and then we thought, oh, we should just ship that. and and then there's the X Crypto Cycle thing, um, this one is a little more experimental, it's a, it reads what people are saying on X, and it tries to place the market in a cycle, like are we in the, the euphoric phase or the boring phase. I don't think it's accurate enough yet, to be honest, I'd call it a toy, a fun toy, and we say that in the product.

okay so what doesn't work, because I think that's the the more interesting part of any talk like this. number one, the thing I keep complaining about, it still doesn't feel proactive enough. like right now Kestrel waits for you, you have to come to it, and what I want is that it, it notices something at three in the morning and and says hey, this wallet you were looking at just moved four point two million into an exchange, and and you decide. we have a version of that, but it's noisy, it pinged people like fifteen times a day in the beta and, uh, a couple of people turned it off and one person told us it was, quote, worse than my ex. so, yeah. we pulled it back. number two is coverage, we're really good on, on Ethereum and Solana, and we're okay on a few others, but anything small or new, we can't really label the wallets, so the answers get thin, and I'd rather it say I don't know than make something up.

and number three is the one I'm kind of embarrassed about, which is the docs. we we have an API, a few of the bigger users are already using it, but the documentation is, it's half written, it's in a doc that only three people can find. so we need to ship the API docs by next month, that's, that's a real commitment, I'm saying it on a stage so now I have to do it. um and I think related to that, we decided to kill the, the old dashboard export feature, the one that made a PDF. nobody used it, like I looked, it was used maybe forty times total, and it was costing us a lot of weird bugs. so that's gone as of, uh, as of last week. and and I know somebody's going to email me about it, and that's fine, I'll tell them to use the API.

so a bit on the roadmap now, and I'll be honest it's not, it's not a fixed thing, it changes basically every few weeks. but the big idea for twenty twenty six is that we want Kestrel to be less of a chat box and more of an agent that, that actually works while you sleep. so you tell it, I care about, I don't know, Zcash and a couple of perps on Solana, and I I only want to hear about it if something is really unusual. and then it watches. and the hard part isn't the watching, the watching is easy, it's the deciding what's worth interrupting you for. and we don't have a good answer yet. we've tried a bunch of thresholds, we've tried letting the model decide, and the model is, it's too eager, it thinks everything is important, kind of like an intern, right? so I think what we'll end up with is a mix, where you set a budget, like, tell me at most three things a day, and it has to spend that budget wisely.

and someone asked me earlier about privacy coins, specifically whether we can say anything useful about Zcash, and honestly the answer is not much. like the whole point is you can't see the flows, so we can show you the transparent side, the shielded side we just can't, and I don't want to pretend we can. we'd rather show a big blank space with a note that says this is not visible than guess. um, another question was about whether Novalit, the company I mean, is going to raise money, and I I can't really talk about that, I'm not sure what I'm allowed to say, so I'll just say we're, we're in a fine place and we're hiring, and and leave it there. we have, uh, nine people now, we were five at launch.

the other thing on the plan, which I'm kind of excited about, is the, the shared workspaces. right now everybody uses Kestrel alone, but a lot of people trade in little groups, like six or seven friends, or a small desk, and they paste screenshots at each other all day. so we want a place where the group shares a watchlist and the agent's notes, and you can see what everybody asked. I don't think it's going to be huge, I'd guess maybe ten percent of users, but those are the people who pay, so, you know. and we're going to start with the, the Telegram groups because that's already where it's happening. a thing I haven't figured out is permissions, who can change the watchlist, who can mute the agent. we'll probably get it wrong the first time. so if anybody here has opinions, uh, find me later, I'm the one with the terrible jacket. oh and and there's also the question of whether the agent should write to the group at all, or only to you, and I I don't have a view yet. one of our beta people said she'd mute it in about a day if it talked too much, which, fair, I would too, and that's kind of the whole risk with anything proactive, you know, it has to earn the right to interrupt.

okay, I think I have maybe five minutes, so let me do a couple of quick ones. somebody asked about pricing. so right now there's a free tier and it's, it's limited by how many questions you can ask a day, and then there's a paid one that's, uh, around thirty dollars a month, and that's, I think we're going to change that, because the people who use the notebook, the, the backtest stuff, cost us way more than the people who just chat. so probably we'll split it, like a cheap plan and a, a heavier plan. I don't know the numbers yet, I'm not going to make one up, I've been burned before. and another one was can people trust the labels. and the answer is, trust but click through, right? if you see a label on a wallet that says fund or market maker, we show you why we think so, and and it's sometimes wrong, I'd say we're wrong maybe, uh, five to ten percent of the time, and when you tell us, we fix it the same day. so that's, that's about all I have. thank you, really, and, um, come find me, I have stickers.

last thing and then I'll let you go to lunch, I promise. one of the nicest things that happened this year was that a user, a guy I've never met, he he wrote this long thread saying he'd stopped trading on feelings and started writing down a rule and backtesting it in the notebook first, and and he said it cut his losses by something like thirty percent. I can't verify that, I'm not going to put it on a slide, but, it's why we do this, right? we're not trying to give people alpha, I think that word is kind of, it's a bit silly, we're trying to make people a little less dumb about what they're doing. okay. that's it. thank you.

hi everyone, um, so I'm Priya, I run product at Ledgerline, and, and what I'm going to show you today is a thing called Halcyon, well, Halcyan is how the speech thing on my phone writes it, so, whatever. so Halcyon is, it's an AI trading copilot, but I, I really hate that word copilot because everyone says it. what it actually does is it, it watches DeFi positions for you. like if you have money in, I don't know, three lending protocols and a couple of liquidity pools, you probably don't know your real risk, right? you know your balance but you don't know, like, what happens if the price drops twenty percent. and so Halcyon builds that picture, and it's a, kind of a, a stress test you can talk to. we started on this about eighteen months ago, and um, the first thing we built was not even AI, it was just a spreadsheet, a very ugly spreadsheet.

and the reason I bring up the spreadsheet is because that's where we learned the, the real problem, which is that people don't want a number, they want to know what to do. so we had this risk score, it said sixty two, and and users would come back and say okay, but is sixty two bad? and we didn't have an answer, we, we literally didn't. so that's when we added the language model, and the idea was, it explains the score. like, it says your risk is mostly because seventy percent of your funds are in one pool and that pool is thin. and that was the moment, I think, that things clicked, because explanation, it turns out, is the product. I'm not sure we understood that before. and and our early users, there were about forty of them, they were friends basically, they kept saying this is the first time I understood my own portfolio.

so let me walk through the main screens. um this first one is the position map, and I I know it looks busy, but the idea is every protocol you're in is a box, and the box is red if something is close to a liquidation, and green if it's, you know, fine. and so you can see at a glance, okay, that one is in trouble. we get this from reading the wallet directly, you just paste in an address, there's no connect, there's no signing, which was a big decision for us. a lot of people at Ledgerline wanted a wallet connect button because it's easier, and and I said no, because the first time someone connects a wallet to a thing they found on the internet and loses money, we're done. so it's read only, and that also means we can't, we can't do anything bad even if we wanted to. so, that was one of those decisions that felt slow at the time but I think it was right.

the second screen is where Hal sion, sorry, Halcyon, talks to you. and and this is the part people think is magic, but it's mostly plumbing. you ask what happens if Ethereum drops thirty percent, and it doesn't just guess, it actually reruns the numbers for each of your positions, with the real collateral ratios, and then the model reads the result and writes it up in plain English. so the model never does the math itself, I'd like to be really clear on that, because we tried it, we tried letting it do the math, and it was wrong a lot. like one time it told a user they'd be liquidated at a price that was, I don't know, four hundred dollars off. and that user, to be fair, noticed. so now the numbers always come from code, and the words come from the model. and I think that split is, it's something other people should copy.

we also have the perps view, which is newer, and, uh, it's not as polished. if you're running leveraged positions, perps, it shows you your funding costs over time, and it flags when you're paying a lot to hold something. one of our users found out he'd paid something like four hundred dollars in funding on a position he'd basically forgotten about, and he was pretty upset, but with us, not at himself, which, hm. no, he was grateful, he was grateful. so that's the view. what it doesn't do, I should say, is tell you when to close. we don't give advice like that. we say here's the cost, here's the risk, and you decide. I mean, we've talked about adding a nudge, and I'm not sure if that's the right thing, there's a regulatory side to it that I don't really understand yet, so we're staying away for now.

and and the last screen is settings, which sounds boring, but there's one thing in there I want to mention, which is the, the risk limits. so you can tell Hal sion, sorry, Halcyon, I don't want any single pool to be more than, say, thirty percent of my money, and and it will tell you when you're over. that was one of the first features users asked for and we we kind of ignored it for months because we thought it was too simple. and and then we shipped it in an afternoon and it's, it's one of the most used things. so, I think there's a lesson there about simple stuff, about not being too clever, um, I keep relearning it. anyway, that's the tour, I'm not sure if it was too fast.

so the numbers. everybody wants the numbers. we have about, uh, eleven thousand active users, and I'd say, I'd say maybe nine hundred of those are paying, so it's a pretty small business honestly. it's not, it's not the kind of thing where you'd see a chart go up and to the right, it's more like a staircase. what's interesting is that the, the weekly digest is what drives most of the usage. so every Monday Halcyon sends you a summary of your positions, what changed, what's riskier, and people open that, I think it's like sixty percent open rate, which is, for email, that's crazy. and then maybe a third of them click through to the app. so I think the product is, a lot of the time, an email. which, as a product person, is a little humbling, right? we built all these screens and the thing people love is a paragraph.

and since we saw that, we started putting the digest in other places. we tried Slack, uh, because a few desks wanted it in their channel, and that worked fine. we also tried a voice version, which, um, I'll be honest, it did not work. like we thought people would listen to their portfolio on the way to work and nobody did. I think we had, I don't know, ninety listens in a month and half of them were us. so we we killed that, that was an easy decision. and and the lesson there I think is, don't build the thing that sounds cool in the meeting. build the thing where you can already see people doing a clumsy version by hand. and the clumsy version of the digest was people screenshotting their positions and posting them to a group chat, so, we knew.

so what's next. um I'd say three things. one is alerts that are actually good, because right now we alert on, on thresholds, like your health factor went under one point five, and it's, it's fine but it's dumb. what I want is it says something looks different about this pool, the liquidity is draining faster than usual. that's harder. two is more chains, we're really only on a couple right now, and people keep asking for more, and, and I don't think we can say yes to all of them. three is the API, because some funds want to pull this into their own tools. and we don't have docs for that yet, we have a, a half page, so that's a to do for this quarter. we need to write them properly and probably get someone outside to try them, because everything seems obvious when you built it.

okay let me talk about the part that I think is actually hard, which is trust. because we, we put an LLM in front of people's money, and and that's a little scary. so what do we do. first, as I said, the math is code. second, every claim in the explanation has to point at a number that the code produced, and if it doesn't, we drop the sentence. we call it the receipts rule. it's, it's not perfect, sometimes the model sneaks in a vague sentence like this pool looks risky and we can't really catch every one of those. but it's a lot better than nothing. and third, we have a, a test set, it's about, I think two hundred portfolios that we made up, and we run every model change against it, and we check does it hallucinate, does it contradict the numbers. when we switched to a smaller model last spring, we saw the contradictions go up, like from one percent to maybe four, and we didn't ship it. we kept the bigger one.

and I, I want to say, a friend at Nova lith, they're another team doing something kind of similar, they told me they don't run any benchmark like that, they just look at the outputs by hand, and I thought, wow, okay. which, I mean, it works when you're small, but I I can't see how it works when you have thousands of users. so we spend, uh, I don't know, maybe twenty percent of our engineering time on evals. it's not glamorous. nobody tweets about it. but if I had to pick one thing that I'd tell a new team, it's that, make the test set early, even if it's bad, and and keep adding the failures to it. we have a thing where every time a user reports a wrong answer, it becomes a test case the same day. and over time, you know, you stop having the same bug twice. that's, that's the whole trick.

there was a question before about whether we use a hosted model or run our own. so right now it's hosted, we call an API, and we, we send only the computed numbers, not the wallet address, which was a privacy thing that our one lawyer really cared about. and I I don't think that's going to change soon, running our own model would be a big project and I'm not convinced it would be better. but we are looking at a small model for the cheap stuff, like classifying what question you asked, which doesn't need the big brain. and and honestly the cost is not the problem right now, it's latency, people feel it when it takes more than, say, eight seconds. and yeah, that's that, I think, on that. someone in the back had a hand up?

oh, and a quick thing I forgot, on the evals, about the judge. so we we use a second model to grade the first one, which a lot of people do, and and I want to say it's not magic, we found it agrees with a human maybe, uh, eighty five percent of the time, and the other fifteen it's, it's often too nice. it likes answers that sound confident. so we we added a few hand written checks that don't use a model at all, like does every number in the text appear in the data, and and those catch the worst stuff. I don't think you can fully trust a model to grade a model, not yet, it's something we keep an eye on, and and we spot check about fifty a week by hand, which is, yeah, it's tedious, but it's, it's the real signal.

yeah so the question was whether Halcyon can see across chains, like if I bridge something, does it know it's the same money. and and the honest answer is mostly no. we see each chain separately and we stitch them together if we can tell, you know, that one wallet bridged to another, but it's, it's heuristic, it's a guess, and we don't want to show a guess as if it's a fact. so in the position map there's a little dotted line for I think this is linked, and a solid line for we know. and and the dotted ones are maybe, I don't know, seventy percent right? so it's, it's something we flag but we don't build features on top of, yet. and another person asked about wallets that are shared by multiple people, like a team treasury. we can't really handle that, because we show one view per address, and the, the permissions part I mentioned, who sees what, that's not built. so that's honestly a gap.

okay and, uh, since this is the Q and A part, someone else asked what was the worst thing that's happened. and, hm. so, there was an incident in the summer where a price feed we depend on went stale for about forty minutes, and and Halcyon told a bunch of people their positions were safe when they were not. nobody lost money, as far as we know, but we, we found out because a user posted a screenshot and said this doesn't look right. and so we wrote it up, publicly, and we added a check that says if the data is older than five minutes, we show a big banner and we don't make claims. which seems obvious in hindsight. and and I think the thing I learned is that the AI part wasn't the failure, it was the boring data pipe, which is, I think, usually where it breaks.

so for next quarter, we've decided, well, mostly decided, we're going to stop adding chains and focus on making the, the existing ones really solid, because I think we've been spreading ourselves too thin. we're also going to hire a, a data engineer, which I should have done six months ago. and we're going to do a, an actual launch of the API with docs and a changelog. and if I'm honest the thing I'm most worried about is, uh, is whether people will still care in a quiet market. everybody's here because things are loud, and and when it gets boring, will they still want to look at their risk? I don't know. I don't think I can answer that. but I'd rather build the thing for the boring market, because that's when you find out who's real. and also, um, one small thing we want to do is a, a public status page, because after the stale feed thing a few people said they'd never know when the data is bad, and and honestly neither would I, if I was them. it's not a big project, maybe a week, but it's the kind of thing that never gets prioritized, so I'm saying it out loud so someone holds me to it. okay, thank you all, that's my time.

alright, so, hi, uh, can everyone hear me, okay good. I'm Marcus, I'm the, the head of product at Bright fen, and and I'm going to talk about Tessellate for the next, I think, twenty five minutes, and then there's time for questions. so Tessellate, some people write it Tesselate with one L, we've never fixed that on the website, it's, it's a trading intelligence platform, which is a very corporate way of saying we take a ton of messy data and make it useful to a human. um the, the company's been around for about, hm, three years, but Tessellate itself is more like fourteen months old. before that we were a data vendor, we sold feeds, like raw feeds, to funds, and honestly it was a good business, but it was a boring business, and and nobody who bought the feed was happy, because they all had to build the same stuff on top, over and over, right? every fund had one or two engineers whose entire job was cleaning our data. and I think that was when somebody said, why don't we just do the cleaning.

so that's what Tessellate is. and and the first customer was actually an accident, a small fund, about three hundred million under management, they they came to us and said we don't want the feed anymore, we want the answers. and we said, uh, what answers? and they said, like, tell me every morning what changed overnight. and so the first version of the product was an email. literally an email, and I wrote half of it by hand for a while, I'm not proud of that. and then we automated it, with a model, and and the first few outputs were, they were just wrong in funny ways. it would say funding rates had gone up when they'd gone down, it mixed up two tokens with similar tickers, once it described a wallet as a person, like it said he sold, I think, a guy named, it invented a name. so we spent the first four months just on, um, making it boring and correct.

and then the thing that changed our trajectory a bit was a bot, a little Telegram bot, we called it Pinglord, uh, some people hear Ping lord, two words, either way. and what Pinglord did is, you could ask it a question in a group chat, like what's going on with Zcash today, or whatever, and it would answer right there, with a chart. and we we built it in about a weekend for an internal demo, it was not supposed to go out. but one of our customers saw it and said can I have that, and then their whole desk wanted it, and within two months it had, I don't know, forty groups using it. and the weird part was they didn't use the main product anymore, they just used the bot. so now we're kind of a company with a product that, that nobody really opens and a bot everyone loves. and we're still figuring out what that means, honestly. I don't think we have a clean answer, and and my co founder thinks it's fine, I'm less sure.

so let me show you the actual product, because I've been talking for a while. okay, this is the home screen, and, and what you see at the top is what we call the morning brief, which is that original email, but in the app. under that is the Wail Radar, which is spelled whale, W H A L E, but the speech to text, whatever it is on this laptop, keeps writing it differently, so I'm just going to go with it. and Whale Radar is, it's a map of, of big wallet activity, like the biggest movements in the last, you can pick, an hour, a day. and each dot is a wallet or a group of wallets, and and the size is how much money, and the color is whether they're buying or selling. it's kind of hypnotic, I'll be honest, we have people who just leave it open on a second monitor all day and I I don't think that's a good use of anybody's time but, it's pretty.

and if you click a dot you get the profile of that wallet, and this is where the Smart Money labels come in. so we we have a, a model that tries to classify what kind of wallet it is, like is it an exchange, a fund, a, a market maker, somebody's cold storage, or a regular person. and and we're about, um, eighty percent right on that, which sounds low, but I think it's, it's actually better than people can do by hand. and we show the confidence, we don't hide it. so you'll see likely fund, sixty percent, and that's the system saying I'm not sure. the first version didn't have that and customers were, were angry because they trusted the label and it was wrong. so we added the confidence and the complaints went down, I think they went down like, a lot, I don't have the number, but I remember the support channel got really quiet.

okay, and this next part is the, the part that I'm most proud of but it's also the part that's most broken, so, you know, take that as you will. it's a thing called the thesis builder. you write down an idea in plain words, like I think funding on these perps is going to flip positive this week, and it turns that into a set of checks, and then it, it monitors them and tells you if the idea is playing out. so it's a bit like a backtest but forward in time. and the broken part is that, um, the language to check translation is not reliable, so sometimes you say one thing and it watches a slightly different thing, and and you don't know. we show you the checks it came up with and you have to approve them, that's the guardrail, but most people don't read them, they just click okay. so, it's, it's a UX problem and a trust problem at the same time and I'm not sure we're solving it.

so now, how do we build this, because I know a few of you are engineers. the stack is, uh, honestly not that interesting, there's a, a stream of on chain events coming in, we normalize them, we label them, and then there's an agent layer on top that can call tools, and the tools are things like get wallet history, get funding rates, run a query. and and the agent is not one big model, it's, it's several small steps, like there's a planner, then there are the tool calls, then there's a writer that turns it into words. and the reason is, when we used one big prompt it, it kind of drifted, it would forget what it was doing half way through, and and splitting it up made each part easy to test. we looked at a, a competitor, I think they call theirs Kestrel, and we noticed they do something similar, so, so I think everyone ends up in the same place.
